Carchemish
KAR-kem-ish
n. (proper, a city on the Euphrates)
Hebrew Karkemiysh, a fortress city commanding the chief crossing of the upper Euphrates. It appears three times in the Authorized Version, and each time it marks a hinge on which the history of nations turned.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah names it in the Assyrian's boast, as one of the cities that had fallen and proved that no city could stand: “Is not Calno as Carchemish? is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus?” (Isaiah 10:9). A century later it is the destination of the march that killed Josiah: “when Josiah had prepared the temple, Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates: and Josiah went out against him” (2 Chronicles 35:20) — and Josiah, warned by Necho not to meddle, disguised himself, fought, and was shot at Megiddo. Then Jeremiah dates the collapse of Egypt to the same place: his oracle is “against the army of Pharaohnecho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah” (Jeremiah 46:2). One ford on one river, and the empire that ruled the world changed hands there.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a city upon the river Euphrates, the site of the battle in which Nebuchadrezzar smote the army of Pharaoh-necho.

expand to see more

EUPHRATES, n. One of the great rivers of western Asia, rising in Armenia and flowing to the Persian gulf; a boundary of the promised land.

FORD, n. A place in a river or other water where it may be passed by man or beast on foot, or by wading.

EMPIRE, n. Supreme power in governing; imperial power; the territories subject to an emperor.

BATTLE, n. A fight or encounter between enemies, or opposing armies; an engagement.

OVERRULE, v.t. To influence or control by predominant power; to govern with high authority.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 10:9 — "Is not Calno as Carchemish? is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus?"

2 Chronicles 35:20 — "After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates: and Josiah went out against him."

Jeremiah 46:2 — "Against Egypt, against the army of Pharaohnecho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah."

2 Chronicles 35:22 — "Nevertheless Josiah would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself, that he might fight with him, and hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and came to fight in the valley of Megiddo."

Modern Corruption

World history is narrated as the product of armies and interests alone; Scripture attaches the same battles to God's purpose, and records that Josiah died because he would not hear a warning that came through a pagan king.

expand to see more

Carchemish is a fixed point in secular chronology, and the Bible treats it as a fixed point in the government of God. Isaiah has the Assyrian boasting of it and then declares that Assyria is the rod of God's anger, a tool that does not know whose hand holds it. Jeremiah dates Nebuchadrezzar's victory there to a regnal year of Jehoiakim, tying the fall of Egypt to the covenant history of Judah. The events are perfectly ordinary as history and perfectly governed as providence, and Scripture never treats those as competing explanations.

The death of Josiah at that hinge is the sober warning. Necho sent word that his quarrel was not with Judah and that God had bidden him make haste, and the chronicler records that Josiah “hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and came to fight in the valley of Megiddo”. The best king since David, who had purged the land and kept the greatest Passover since Samuel, died because he would not hear a true word that came through an unwelcome mouth. Faithfulness in the past does not exempt a man from listening in the present.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Karkemiysh (H3751), Carchemish; Perath (H6578), Euphrates; Nekow (H5224), Necho; Nebuwkadretstsar (H5019), Nebuchadrezzar.

expand to see more

Hebrew Karkemiysh (H3751) — Carchemish, a fortress on the Euphrates crossing.

Hebrew Perath (H6578) — the Euphrates; the river by which the empire changed hands.

Hebrew Nekow (H5224) — Necho, the Pharaoh whose warning Josiah refused.

Hebrew Nebuwkadretstsar (H5019) — Nebuchadrezzar, whom Jeremiah calls God's servant.

Hebrew Megiddow (H4023) — Megiddo, the valley where Josiah was shot.

Usage

"“Is not Calno as Carchemish?” — the Assyrian's boast."

"“Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates”."

"“Which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote” — an empire ends at a ford."
